title: Smooth quotient by a smooth subgroup of a commutative group variety
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. Let $G$ and $H$ be commutative $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] that are smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], separated and of finite type [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions], and geometrically integral, meaning that their base changes to every field extension of $k$ are nonempty integral schemes [def-pc-integral-scheme, def-pc-base-change]. Let $i:H\hookrightarrow G$ be a closed immersion of group schemes. There exist a smooth separated geometrically integral commutative $k$-group scheme $Q$ of finite type and a smooth surjective homomorphism $p:G\to Q$ of finite presentation such that $p\circ i=0$, $i$ identifies $H$ with the scheme-theoretic kernel of $p$, and the morphism
$$G\times_k H\longrightarrow G\times_QG,\qquad(g,h)\longmapsto(g,g+i(h))$$
is an isomorphism [def-pc-fibre-product]. In particular, for every $k$-scheme $T\to Q$, the pullback $G_T\to T$ is faithfully flat and the corresponding morphism $G_T\times_T H_T\to G_T\times_TG_T$ is an isomorphism. Here faithfully flat means flat and surjective, and finite presentation means locally of finite presentation, quasi-compact and quasi-separated [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions].

source.place: Theorem 5.14 (normal-subgroup quotient); Corollary 5.27 (torsor); Proposition 1.63 (smoothness with smooth kernel). Applied to commutative smooth geometrically integral group varieties. Geometric integrality of Q follows after field extension from the surjective quotient and its smoothness.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homogeneous-quotient] with $L=H$ and $j=i$; its hypotheses hold because $G$ is separated and of finite type and $i$ is a closed immersion of group schemes, so $H$ is a closed subgroup scheme of $G$. No normality, smoothness or affineness is needed. Obtain a separated finite-type $k$-scheme $Q$ and a flat, surjective, finitely presented $k$-morphism $p:G\to Q$ such that, for every $k$-scheme $U$ and $g,g'\in G(U)$, $p(g)=p(g')$ in $Q(U)$ if and only if $g'=g+i(h)$ for some $h\in H(U)$. This $h$ is unique: a closed immersion is locally defined by a surjective ring map, so two maps $U\to H$ with equal composites to $G$ agree on each affine open of $U$, hence agree. Therefore $(g,h)\mapsto(g,g+i(h))$ is a bijection $G(U)\times H(U)\to(G\times_QG)(U)$ [def-pc-fibre-product]; its inverse sends $(g,g')$ to $(g,h)$ with $i(h)=g'-g$, and uniqueness makes both maps natural in $U$. Applying [lem-galois-yoneda-fully-faithful] on the category of $k$-schemes, the morphism $\theta:G\times_kH\to G\times_QG$, $(g,h)\mapsto(g,g+i(h))$, is an isomorphism. The one-member family $\{p\}$ is an fpqc covering of $Q$ [def-weil-pbc-fpqc-covering]: $p$ is flat, and for an affine open $V\subseteq Q$ the preimage $p^{-1}(V)$ is quasi-compact because $p$ is quasi-compact, so finitely many affine opens cover it, and their images cover $V$ because $p$ is surjective.

source.place: Theorem 5.28 with Definition 5.20, Proposition 5.24 and Proposition 5.25, printed pp.104-105

proof.text: Universal property with parameters. Let $T$ be a $k$-scheme and $p_T=p\times_k\mathrm{id}_T:G\times_kT\to Q\times_kT$. Since $p_T$ is the base change of $p$ along the projection $Q\times_kT\to Q$, [lem-galois-fpqc-covering-base-change] makes $\{p_T\}$ an fpqc covering of $Q\times_kT$. Its kernel pair $(G\times_kT)\times_{Q\times_kT}(G\times_kT)$ is $(G\times_QG)\times_kT$, which $\theta\times\mathrm{id}_T$ of step 1 identifies with $G\times_kH\times_kT$, the two projections becoming $(g,h,t)\mapsto(g,t)$ and $(g,h,t)\mapsto(g+i(h),t)$. Hence a morphism $a:G\times_kT\to Y$ to a $T$-scheme $Y$ has equal composites with the two projections of the kernel pair exactly when $a(g+i(h),t)=a(g,t)$ on $G\times_kH\times_kT$. For such an $a$ which is a $T$-morphism, [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent] applied to the covering $\{p_T\}$ gives a unique morphism $\bar a:Q\times_kT\to Y$ with $\bar a\circ p_T=a$; it is a $T$-morphism because its composite with $Y\to T$ and the projection $Q\times_kT\to T$ agree after precomposition with $p_T$, so they agree by the uniqueness part of the same lemma applied with target $T$. The uniqueness part also shows that two morphisms out of $Q\times_kT$ which agree after precomposition with $p_T$ are equal.

source.place: Tag 023Q (lemma-fpqc-universal-effective-epimorphisms) for the covering p_T; Milne Proposition 5.21, printed p.104, is the case T = Spec k

proof.text: Write the law on $G$ additively. The map $(g_1,g_2)\mapsto p(g_1+g_2)$ is unchanged when $g_1$ is replaced by $g_1+i(h_1)$. The universal property of step 2 with parameter $T=G$ therefore gives a unique morphism $b:Q\times_kG\to Q$. It is invariant under translation by $H$ in the second variable: after precomposing with $p\times\mathrm{id}_{G\times H}$ the two maps are $p(g_1+g_2+i(h))$ and $p(g_1+g_2)$, equal by commutativity in $G$ and $H$-invariance of $p$; the uniqueness clause of step 2 with $T=G\times_kH$ makes them equal before precomposition. Applying step 2 again, with parameter $T=Q$ and the factors interchanged, gives $m_Q:Q\times_kQ\to Q$ with $m_Q(p(g_1),p(g_2))=p(g_1+g_2)$. The map $g\mapsto p(-g)$ is $H$-invariant since $-(g+i(h))=-g+i(-h)$, so it descends to $v_Q:Q\to Q$. Set $e_Q=p\circ e_G$.

source.place: Proposition 5.12 and the paragraph proving Theorem 5.14 after Theorem 5.28, printed pp.101,105; explicit parameterwise descent

proof.text: Precomposition with each map $p\times\mathrm{id}_T$ is injective on morphisms by the uniqueness clause of step 2. Repeatedly using this injectivity in each variable shows that maps out of $Q^r$ are equal whenever their composites with $p^r:G^r\to Q^r$ are equal. Pull the associativity, commutativity, unit and inverse diagrams for $(m_Q,e_Q,v_Q)$ back along $p^3$, $p^2$, $p$ and $p$, respectively. They become the corresponding identities on $G$, followed by $p$, so they commute. These operations thus define a commutative group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme], and the defining identity for $m_Q$ says that $p$ is a homomorphism.

source.place: Proposition 5.12, printed p.101: checking the group diagrams by the quotient universal property

proof.text: Invariance gives $p\circ i=p\circ e_G\circ(H\to\operatorname{Spec}k)=e_Q\circ(H\to\operatorname{Spec}k)$, that is $p\circ i=0$. For a $k$-scheme $U$ and $g\in G(U)$, step 1 with $g'=0$ shows that $p(g)=e_Q$ exactly when $g=i(h)$ for a unique $h\in H(U)$, naturally in $U$. Thus $i$ induces a natural bijection from $H(U)$ to the $U$-points of $\ker p=G\times_{Q,p,e_Q}\operatorname{Spec}k$ [def-sc-group-scheme], and [lem-galois-yoneda-fully-faithful] identifies $i$ with the scheme-theoretic kernel inclusion. The isomorphism $\theta:G\times_kH\simeq G\times_QG$ of the statement is the one of step 1.

source.place: Proposition 5.24, printed pp.104-105, with Definition 1.1 and the scheme-theoretic kernel of Section 1(e)

proof.text: The base change of $p:G\to Q$ along itself, namely the second projection $G\times_QG\to G$, is identified by $\theta$ with $G\times_kH\to G$, $(g,h)\mapsto g+i(h)$. This is the first projection $G\times_kH\to G$ composed with the automorphism $(g,h)\mapsto(g+i(h),h)$ of $G\times_kH$ (inverse $(g,h)\mapsto(g-i(h),h)$), and the first projection is smooth by [lem-pc-proper-base-change](2), since $H\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth. The cover $p$ is flat, quasi-compact and surjective by step 1, so [lem-trf-smooth-fpqc-base-descent] applied with $f=p$ and $g=p$ makes $p$ smooth. To prove $Q$ smooth over $k$, apply [lem-sbc-smooth-flat-surjective-source-descent] with $q=p$ and $f:Q\to\operatorname{Spec}k$: $p$ is flat, surjective and locally of finite presentation, and $f\circ p:G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth by hypothesis.

source.place: Tag 02VL (lemma-descending-property-smooth); Tag 05B5 (lemma-smooth-permanence), smooth case; Milne Proposition 1.62 and Proposition 1.63

proof.text: For every field extension $K/k$, [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-base-change] makes $p_K:G_K\to Q_K$ surjective. Since $G$ is geometrically integral, $G_K$ is nonempty and irreducible. Thus $Q_K$ is nonempty and irreducible: if it were the union of two proper closed subsets, their inverse images under the continuous surjection would be two proper closed subsets covering $G_K$. Smoothness of $Q\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ implies that $Q$ is geometrically reduced by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced], hence $Q_K$ is reduced. It is therefore integral by [def-pc-integral-scheme]. As $K$ was arbitrary, $Q$ is geometrically integral.

Finally take an arbitrary $k$-scheme $T\to Q$. The projection $G_T=G\times_QT\to T$ is flat by [lem-weil-pbc-flat-morphism-base-change] and surjective by [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-base-change], so it is faithfully flat. Pull back $\theta$ along $T\to Q$. The fibre-product universal property identifies its two sides with $G_T\times_TH_T$ and $G_T\times_TG_T$, where $H_T=H\times_kT$, and the pulled-back map is exactly $(g,h)\mapsto(g,g+i_T(h))$. Pullback preserves an isomorphism because the pullback of its inverse is an inverse. This proves the last clause with the stated map, including for empty or nonreduced $T$.
